newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmiri leader warns Delhi against poll rigging.
newsitem.headline: Kashmiri leader warns Delhi against poll rigging.

text.p: Former Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah warned New Delhi on Wednesday that alleged rigging of state polls by government-backed militias would lead the state to set up its own election commission.

Abdullah, widely tipped to become chief minister of Indian-ruled Jammu and Kashmir after this month's four-stage assembly polls, told a public rally in the summer capital of Srinagar that he would seek more autonomy from Delhi.
"Kashmir is the crown of India, please do not wear it around your feet," Abdullah told the tightly guarded meeting of some 600 cheering supporters of his National Conference party.
He said government-backed militias had rigged the first two phases of the polls in some districts.

"We are told that the Indian Election Commission is an independent body. We will test that claim in Kashmir. If things are not set right, Kashmir will be forced to pull out of the Election Commision," he said to loud applause.

The government says the first two phases of the elections on September 7 and 16 were fair and peaceful. The next two rounds are on September 21 and 30. Results are expected in the first week of October.
Kashmir had its own election commission before a pact with New Delhi in 1952 diluted some of the state's privileges. Abdullah's aides said he could be hinting at going back to the pre-pact position.

The National Conference boycotted India's parliamentary elections in May but agreed to contest the assembly polls after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda promised to discuss greater autonomy for Kashmir with the new state government.
India's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) opposes special privileges for the country's only state where Moslems are in a majority.

A BJP deputy told reporters in Srinagar on Wednesday his party would block the two-thirds majority needed by parliament to amend the constitution for Kashmir. The BJP has the support of 192 deputies in the 545-member parliament.

Abdullah said his quest for more autonomy for Kashmir had been foiled by politicians in Delhi on the grounds that he was not a "dependable" man to lead the state, which has been the scene of two of India's three wars with Pakistan since independence from Britain in 1947.
"I am not a slave of Delhi, never was and never will be," Abdullah said. "We are a part of India and a strong part of India."
His strained relations with successive Indian governments led to his resignation as chief minister in January 1990, paving the way for direct rule from Delhi.
Indian politicians have often accused Abdullah of being soft towards Kashmiri separatists, but Abdullah sought to play this down in his speech on Wednesday.
"The gulf of mistrust between Delhi and Kashmir had brought us to the brink of disaster," he said. "Pakistan fully exploited the situation."
India accuses Pakistan of training and arming Kashmiri separatists. Islamabad say it gives them only political suport.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed since 1990, when simmering discontent against Indian rule turned into an armed revolt in the Kashmir valley.
